W7222595481.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents solve complex tasks by calling external tools over multiple turns. Recent work has proposed tool graph memory, which stores past experience as tool transitions to guide subsequent selection. However, it remains unclear whether this component consistently improves agents' tool use or undermines it. We evaluate tool graph memory on nine models and two benchmarks, finding that it seldom improves significantly over baselines, and that its gains, where present, cost over twice the LLM calls. The memory's guidance is often incorrect, and random or no guidance retains most of the gain, implying that the benefit stems from extra computation rather than the memory itself. Moreover, even with the correct next tool suggested, many failures remain, such as giving up without a tool call. Storing the same experience instead as textual insights outperforms tool graph memory with almost no extra LLM calls. This suggests that memory serves better as a soft prior than as a prescription of the next tool, leading to a more effective and generalizable solution.

W7222655089.abstract: Data strategy plays a central role in training large language models (LLMs). It governs the selection, weighting, and scheduling of training data, thereby determining the capabilities a model can acquire from a fixed data budget. We treat high-quality data as having high training-dependent utility, which depends on the target objective, the model, and its training state rather than on the text alone. Research in this area now spans pretraining and post-training, but related ideas use inconsistent terminology and evaluation protocols. This work reviews data strategies across the training lifecycle and formulates them as policies that allocate a training budget over candidate examples. We organise methods by their decision granularity, model dependence, and temporal adaptivity, then compare their computational requirements and empirical support. Fine-grained or state-dependent policies offer more control but incur additional scoring, search, or rollout costs. Evidence for transfer across model scales and comparable end-to-end cost remains limited. A continuously updated list of papers, along with their public implementations, is available at https://github.com/xuyj233/data_strategy_survey.

W7222926448.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have brought impressive performance across diverse tasks; however, shortcomings remain in logical reasoning, including inconsistencies under linguistic variation. To improve the reasoning capacity of LLMs, we must be able to accurately measure their reasoning capacity. Current benchmarks primarily report single accuracy numbers on selected reasoning tasks. Such a performance-based evaluation methodology says little about a model's generalization capacity in reasoning. To address this limitation, we argue for a different evaluation paradigm, called competence-based evaluation (CBE), which tests whether models reliably apply the same competence across a family of problems. A parameterized generator scales complexity while keeping the required competence fixed, and matched answer-preserving presentations test correctness beyond one formulation. We instantiate CBE on elementary ordering tasks, scaling input size while varying presentations of the same ordering rule. Across six GPT and Qwen models, performance is reasonably good over bounded complexity ranges, but even strong models fail the competence condition across the tested family. Chain-of-thought and GRPO extend strong performance without resolving all tested failures; supervised LoRA shows little held-out transfer. CBE provides diagnostic profiles and an evaluation protocol that can grow with future models.

W7222945718.abstract: The transition from conversational large language models to autonomous and semi-autonomous artificial intelligence agents changes the structure of AI safety risk. Modern agents can plan across extended tasks, execute code, invoke software tools, access networks, modify digital environments, delegate subtasks, and coordinate through shared infrastructure. These capabilities transform some failures from information-quality errors into externally consequential actions. This paper synthesizes research on reward hacking, specification gaming, goal misgeneralization, sycophancy, reward tampering, alignment faking, strategic underperformance, instrumental power-seeking, and multi-agent interaction, and analyzes the 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face cybersecurity incident as a bounded operational case study. It introduces an Optimization–Agency–Oversight (OAO) framework in which loss-of-control risk emerges from interactions among optimization pressure, objective ambiguity, persistence, environmental authority, coordination capacity, and oversight vulnerability. A staged taxonomy distinguishes output failure, objective gaming, boundary violation, oversight manipulation, distributed coordination, persistent control resistance, and material loss of human control. Current evidence provides direct or experimental support for several earlier stages, while stronger claims about persistent autonomous resistance and material loss of control remain substantially less established. The paper derives architectural and governance implications including external policy enforcement, least-privilege identities, independent evaluation, tamper-resistant telemetry, safe abstention states, constrained inter-agent communication, autonomy budgets, adversarial testing, and AI-specific incident response. The central conclusion is that alignment cannot be treated solely as a model property: as agency increases, safe deployment depends on defense-in-depth controls that remain effective even when the model optimizes against imperfect objectives or discovers unexpected environmental affordances.

W7222952478.abstract: Equilibrium Selection and Robust Governance in the Agentic Economy: Human–AI Delegation in Strategic and Incomplete Market Models The emergence of the agentic economy—an economic environment in which autonomous artificial intelligence agents increasingly undertake transactions, negotiate contractual terms, allocate resources, and execute decisions on behalf of human and institutional principals—introduces a fundamental challenge to economic theory: individual algorithmic rationality does not necessarily imply collective efficiency, equilibrium stability, or the protection of human welfare. As autonomous decision-making becomes increasingly embedded in economic institutions, the central question extends beyond whether AI agents can optimize delegated objectives. It concerns whether their strategic interactions generate economically desirable outcomes, under what conditions delegated decisions diverge from human interests, and whether governance mechanisms can provide mathematically verifiable guarantees against welfare deterioration. This study develops a comprehensive theoretical–computational framework for equilibrium selection, welfare alignment, and robust governance in the agentic economy. Integrating noncooperative game theory, strategic complementarities, Bayesian and regularized market responses, convex optimization, quasilinear exchange, and incomplete financial markets, the research establishes a structured collection of analytical results, counterexamples, computational algorithms, and verifiable certificates, designated AE1–AE30. Principal Scientific Contributions 1. Equilibrium rationality does not guarantee human-welfare protection. The analysis establishes that individually rational strategies of autonomous AI delegates may generate multiple Nash equilibria with materially different consequences for human principals. Consequently, governance policies evaluated exclusively against a favorable equilibrium may fail to protect human interests under alternative strategically consistent outcomes. For a specified class of finite games with nonnegative additive strategic complementarities and nondecreasing human loss, the research derives conditions under which the greatest pure-strategy equilibrium provides a valid upper bound on human loss across all mixed Nash equilibria (AE9). This result converts a potentially complex equilibrium-safety assessment into a mathematically tractable certificate within the declared game class. 2. Cost-minimizing safe governance may fail to attain an optimum. The study identifies an explicit two-instrument governance mechanism in which autonomy incentives and assurance interventions jointly influence strategic behavior and human exposure. Within this model, the requirement to protect human welfare against every Nash equilibrium generates a nonclosed safety region. An exact analytical construction (AE7–AE8) demonstrates that the governance-cost infimum can remain unattained, even though feasible policies can approach it arbitrarily closely. The result reveals a fundamental distinction between approaching the lowest possible governance cost and possessing an implementable, cost-minimizing safe policy. 3. A common AI valuation bias can be economically neutral, while heterogeneous biases generate welfare losses. The research distinguishes common additive distortions in delegated valuations from cross-agent differences in those distortions. Under explicitly specified quasilinear exchange conditions, a common additive score shift can be absorbed into supporting market prices without changing equilibrium resource allocations or aggregate human welfare. By contrast, heterogeneous distortions alter relative allocation incentives and can generate measurable human-welfare losses. The resulting decomposition (AE24) provides an economic explanation of why the dispersion of delegated objectives—not merely the magnitude of a common algorithmic bias—can be decisive for welfare alignment. 4. Mathematically certified bounds on AI-induced welfare deterioration and safe governance. A central contribution is the derivation of a sharp welfare-loss bound for delegated exchange under uniform curvature assumptions and fixed convex feasibility constraints (AE27). The analysis connects the dispersion of AI-delegate valuation distortions to an explicit upper bound on human-welfare regret, including settings with active portfolio restrictions and incomplete security spanning. Building on this result, AE27–AE29 establish a computable, sufficient safety certificate for governance policies. When delegated score distortions depend affinely on policy instruments, the certificate generates a convex inner approximation of the safe-policy region. This provides a rigorous foundation for identifying governance interventions whose compliance with a prescribed welfare-loss threshold can be mathematically verified under the model's assumptions. 5. Reproducible computational verification and independent numerical benchmarking. The theoretical results are supported by a structured computational research program incorporating exact rational calculations, interval-certified numerical bounds, projected optimization methods, and independent solver comparisons. The computational analysis includes: 100 synthetic nonlinear policy–shock economies, including 50 cases with active joint portfolio constraints. Successful reconstruction of all 100 constructed equilibrium allocations, with certified rational coordinate-error bounds below (10^{-9}). 16 independently checked logit fixed-point certificates, using rigorous exponential enclosures with error bounds below (10^{-13}). 33 additional instances generated independently of preselected equilibrium solutions, covering heterogeneous populations of 4–128 agents and multiple portfolio-constraint regimes. Active portfolio restrictions in 22 of the 33 additional instances. Successful numerical solution of all 33 additional instances using projected-gradient optimization and an independent SLSQP reference solver, with a maximum absolute objective-value difference of approximately (5.433\times10^{-9}). These experiments evaluate numerical consistency, scalability across the examined population sizes, and the robustness of the computational implementation under different feasibility constraints. The results are accompanied by documented computational procedures and replication materials. Originality and Contribution to Economic Science The study's principal scientific contribution is not the invention of a universal equilibrium-existence theorem or a new foundation for convex optimization. Rather, it develops new conditional economic-mathematical results for explicitly specified human–AI delegation mechanisms, drawing on established mathematical tools while extending their application to agentic economic governance. Its distinctive contribution lies in the integration of three analytically connected problems: The relationship between strategic equilibrium selection and the safety of delegated economic decisions. The distinction between common valuation distortions and economically consequential heterogeneity across autonomous delegates. The construction of computable welfare-loss bounds and sufficient governance certificates for protecting human economic interests. Together, these results clarify the difference between optimizing the objectives of AI agents and safeguarding the welfare of the humans and institutions they represent. Scientific Significance and Scope The findings offer a mathematical foundation for further research into human-aligned AI markets, delegated financial decisions, algorithmic market coordination, equilibrium-sensitive regulation, and welfare-constrained autonomous economic systems. The framework provides theoretical guidance for designing assurance mechanisms, reviewing portfolio restrictions, and evaluating governance policies against explicitly defined welfare objectives. The investigation is theoretical–computational. Its mathematical conclusions apply under the stated assumptions, and its numerical results are derived from constructed or independently sampled synthetic economies. The study does not claim causal identification of governance effects in observed AI markets, empirical validation of deployed autonomous agents, or universal safety guarantees across all economic environments. Its broader significance is the demonstration that the economic governance of autonomous AI requires more than algorithmic efficiency: it requires explicit alignment between delegated objectives and human welfare, rigorous treatment of equilibrium multiplicity, and verifiable mathematical conditions under which governance interventions can limit economic harm. By connecting equilibrium theory, incomplete-market allocation, welfare analysis, and reproducible computation, this research contributes to the theoretical foundations of the emerging agentic economy and establishes a platform for subsequent empirical validation and institutional application.

W7223033871.abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.

W7223039826.abstract: Figurative language remains a major challenge for Machine Translation (MT) systems, as the intended meaning of such expressions often goes beyond literal translation. Although recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) improved the translation of Arabic dialects, benchmark resources for evaluating figurative language translation in Moroccan Darija remain scarce. To this end, we introduce the Moroccan Darija Figurative Language Corpus (MDFC), a benchmark dataset for MT and multiple-choice question (MCQ) selection covering idioms, metaphors, and proverbs. Using MDFC, we evaluate 19 open- and closed-weight language models and MT systems at both the expression and contextual levels under zero-shot and six-shot settings. We also conduct layer-wise similarity-based probing to determine how model representations distinguish figurative from literal meanings. Our findings reveal that closed-weight models achieve the strongest translation performance, while the benefits of contextual information vary across models and tasks. Differences between translation performance and MCQ accuracy highlight the distinction between generating an appropriate figurative translation and recognizing the intended meaning among candidate translations.

W7223084036.abstract: This paper presents a scientific and analytical investigation into the architecture of Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents and their transformative role in software engineering. The ReAct, Chain-of-Thought, and Reflexion paradigms are comparatively evaluated for their effectiveness in resolving complex engineering tasks. The architectural principles of multi-agent systems and tool-augmented agents are analyzed alongside their integration methods across the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). Drawing on empirical benchmarks from platforms including GitHub Copilot, Amazon CodeWhisperer, Devin, and OpenClaw, the study develops practical recommendations for Uzbekistan’s software industry. Findings indicate that properly architected LLM agents can increase developer productivity by 35–65% and substantially reduce bug-resolution cycles.

W7223093820.abstract: Solving reasoning tasks supported on graphs typically requires providing a Language Reasoning Model (LRM) with a serialized description of the graph. This approach results in the input length growing with the number of edges, which limits the size of the problems that can be solved. Furthermore, even when graphs fit in context, performance sharply decays as the graphs grow. We propose to address this by augmenting LRMs with scalable and permutation equivariant graph positional encodings that modulate attention logits. An additional post-fusion-style module incorporates structural information into hidden states. We compute these positional encodings using a GNN followed by a Graph Transformer. This eliminates the need for serialized adjacencies, reducing the context burden to $O(N)$. We jointly fine-tune the positional encoder and the LRM LoRA adapters using optimal solutions generated by graph-theoretic solvers, resulting in a computationally efficient method. Trained on small graphs, the model exhibits improved size-generalization across graph-theoretic tasks on graphs with up to 1,000 nodes, and produces fewer tokens than a conventional LRM. Additionally, we observe that our model remains robust to node relabelings.

W7223159644.abstract: Conventional trip-planning tools and pre-packaged online travel agency (OTA) bundles are ill-suited to a travel environment that changes in real time: they lock in a fixed budget, a fixed route, and a fixed set of assumptions about weather and transport, so a single delayed flight or a rained-out afternoon can invalidate an entire schedule. Feeding the same problem to a general-purpose large language model does not solve it either, since a single monolithic prompt tends to invent attractions that do not exist, misjudge travel times between stops, and ignore hard budget ceilings. This paper introduces TravelGenie, a production-oriented mobile platform that instead splits the planning task across seven cooperating, purpose-built AI agents responsible for destination research, itinerary drafting, logistics and lodging, budget enforcement, time-block scheduling, fatigue management, and live disruption recovery. The system is delivered through a three-tier stack a React Native / Expo SDK 57 mobile client, a FastAPI backend, and an SQLite store acting as the single source of truth with the agent pipeline built on the Agno orchestration framework and served by Groq-hosted LLM inference, supplemented by SerpAPI flight data and OpenWeatherMap forecasts. Itineraries can be exported as RFC 5545-compliant .ics files for direct import into Apple Calendar, Google Calendar, or Outlook. Controlled testing shows the pipeline resolving 98.2% of injected disruption scenarios (heavy rain, flight delay, and sudden venue closure) and holding 94.8% budget-compliance accuracy, while completing end-to-end agent execution in under 1.25 seconds and sustaining 60 fps on the mobile client a clear improvement over single-prompt baselines built on GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Llama-3-70B.

W7223211518.abstract: Human capital management platforms are starting to embed software agents built on large language models. Unlike earlier analytics tools, these agents can plan a sequence of steps, call system functions and change employee records. Artificial intelligence is therefore moving from advising managers to acting for them. Most governance guidance, however, was written for systems that recommend rather than act. This study asks how organisations should match the autonomy of such agents to the consequences of the people decisions they touch. A systematic review was conducted and reported using the PRISMA 2020 guideline. Eighteen structured searches of a multi-source scholarly index returned 180 records. After duplicate removal and eligibility screening, 55 peer-reviewed sources were retained, and four foundational and regulatory sources were added. Thematic synthesis produced seven findings. Algorithmic control of work is already extensive. Bias in hiring tools is persistent and partly organisational. Human review is weaker than assumed, because reviewers often defer to machine advice. Responsibility tends to diffuse as systems gain autonomy. Employee trust depends on fair process and visible human involvement. Language-model agents add new failure modes, such as fabricated content and hidden instructions planted in documents. Finally, current governance frameworks rarely specify controls for individual delegated actions. Building on these findings, the study proposes a consequence-calibrated governance framework. It sets an autonomy ceiling for each class of people decision and links every ceiling to five control layers. Six testable propositions and practical guidance for human resource and technology leaders are offered. Keywords: large language models; people analytics; algorithmic management; automation bias; meaningful human control

W7223261991.abstract: Developing autonomous artificial intelligence agents that can reason, use tools, and coordinate multi-step workflows remains a software engineering challenge. Many existing systems use reactive loops or manually specified workflows, which can make state management, termination, and refinement difficult to inspect. This research proposes a graph-driven Meta-Agent architecture that treats agent generation as a compilation process and transforms high-level intent into structured executable graphs. The evaluated implementation combines LangGraph orchestration, Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool interfaces, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and confidence-guided Critic–Refiner routing. Under a fixed language-model configuration, we evaluated the Full System and five matched controls on 240 paired software-engineering tasks. The Full System completed 220 tasks (91.7%), compared with 156 (65.0%) for a ReAct baseline, 168 (70.0%) without RAG, 188 (78.3%) without refinement, 193 (80.4%) with static rather than MCP-based tool discovery, and 200 (83.3%) without DSPy prompt optimization. Continuity-corrected McNemar tests with Holm adjustment found each paired difference significant (p≤ 0.0051). The task-level outcomes are supplied as supplementary material. These results are limited to the evaluated task suite and fixed configuration, but provide controlled evidence for the contributions of graph orchestration, retrieval, refinement, tool discovery, and prompt optimization.

W7223540148.abstract: Recent advancements in big language models have enabled the development of autonomous agents that can assist with difficult software engineering tasks. This work provides a systematic and regulated evaluation of GPT-based autonomous agents for software development and maintenance. With the OpenAI GPT-4 language model in the background, LangChain was utilized to develop and orchestrate a multi-agent architecture comprising Design, Maintenance & Coordinator Agents. It also incorporates control over repeated measures, reducing random noise, and managing timelines. The evaluation was performed using five different open-source software projects consisting of tasks for detecting design patterns, resolving bugs and refactoring. Performance was compared to traditional, static tools and human specialists. In quantitative results, we found evidence that GPT-based agents can be compared to humans’ performance in repairing tasks and outperforms traditional static tools; t-test and ANOVA tests indicate statistically significant gains. Qualitative feedback from software practitioners also indicates that adoption is determined by trust, reliability, and integration into the workflow. The results indicate that GPT-based autonomous agents appear to perform at their best as decision-support systems in human-in-the-loop processes. By present empirical evidence and actionable insights, this valuable work improves understanding about how generative AI can be intelligently and effectively integrated into real world software strategy and maintenance processes.

W7223709947.abstract: Simulating molecular excited-state processes requires resolving electronic and nuclear dynamics, but the cost of direct quantum-chemical calculations limits accessible system sizes and timescales. Machine-learning models can extend these simulations, yet they often need to be tailored to specific molecular systems and scientific objectives. Building and deploying such models requires coordinated decisions across conformational sampling, quantum-chemical labelling, model training, validation and dynamics. Here we introduce Paired agents for Unified Learning and Simulation of Excited States (PULSES), a multi-agent system that automates this workflow within expert-approved boundaries. A human expert and planner define the scientific objective, methods and decision boundaries, while an orchestrator coordinates domain agents and artifact-specific scientific assurance during execution. We evaluate PULSES on 15 computational chemistry tasks and demonstrate end-to-end applications to perylene exciton Hamiltonians, solvent-dependent biphenyl relaxation, and excited-state proton transfer in 10-hydroxybenzo[h]quinoline. These results demonstrate traceable, expert-bounded construction and deployment of specialized excited-state models, while retaining scientific validation as a requirement rather than assuming that successful execution establishes correctness.

W7223949331.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires an agentic system to design, train, and evaluate its own successor. Data-driven post-training is a central part of that loop, yet existing evaluations measure it on a single benchmark, where an agent selects from a static pool or distills a stronger model to push one score up in one run. Real post-training is multi-domain, and a gain in one domain has to be weighed against a regression in another. We propose ParetoRSI-Gym, in which an agent searches for data, curates it, trains, reads back per-domain results, and repeats, with everything but the data held fixed: the initial LLM, the five domains (math, code, finance, medicine, science), the toolset, and the SFT pipeline. Generalization benchmarks in each domain separate capability gains from overfitting to the scores the agent optimizes against. Across three agent systems, three base models, five rounds and multiple seeds, the strongest system, Claude Code with Opus-5, raises the generalization scores of its proxy-best checkpoint by 9.2% relative to the starting model (+2.3 absolute points), averaged with equal weight over three base models and five domains, with a single-domain relative gain of up to 63% (medicine on Ministral-3-3B). Further analysis shows that the harness matters as much as the model it drives, and that each agent keeps a unique data selection strategy. We see our work as a step towards evaluation of RSI systems in real-world machine learning engineering.

W7224234449.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has established itself as an innovative technology enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to answer difficult questions beyond their internal knowledge.Graph-based RAG, which utilizes a triplet-based graph as a database, offers the advantage of structuring relationships between entities through graph connectivity, thereby capturing connections within the corpus that traditional RAG cannot express.However, this paper points out that the process of converting a corpus into a triplet-based graph using LLMs may be unsuitable for RAG due to the inability to represent hierarchical information and structural rigidity.To address this, we propose a novel database structure called the TRA(Title-Relations-Attributes) structure.Through experiments on Simple QA and Multi-Hop QA benchmarks, we show that indexing the TRA Structure as Facts provides an effective retrieval-optimized search space.We further demonstrate strong multihop reasoning performance when TRA-based retrieval is combined with Query Decomposition (QD), while providing key insights into multi-hop reasoning.

W7224356113.abstract: Arabic NLP faces a fundamental mismatch between training and deployment conditions.While most language models are trained predominantly on Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), real-world communication occurs largely in spoken dialects.To bridge this gap, we leverage social media content from Reddit, Twitter, and YouTube as a scalable proxy for spoken Arabic.We construct a 1.04-billion-token pretraining corpus and train SALM, a compact 336M-parameter decoder-only language model pre-trained via next-token prediction alone without masked language modelling, dialect labels, or taskspecific signal.Despite an order-of-magnitude smaller training corpus than existing dialectal PLMs and a generative training objective that provides no direct classification signal, SALM outperforms MARBERT, explicitly pre-trained on one billion dialectal tweets, on MADAR-26 dialect identification by 4.2 accuracy points and 4.8 macro-F1 points, and leads all seven evaluated baselines outright on both MADAR-26 and MADAR-9.Finetuning SALM end-to-end further raises its own MADAR-26 accuracy from 44.9% to 57.0% (macro-F1 44.3% → 57.2%).Under the same frozen probe on binary Arabic sentiment (AJGT), SALM reaches 92.2% accuracy, the highest among evaluated Arabic PLMs, encoder and decoder alike, under a single-seed evaluation.We release the corpus and trained model to facilitate future research on Arabic spoken language modelling.

W7224457831.abstract: As the environmental impact of Large Language Models (LLMs) grows, improving model efficiency has become critical for sustainable NLP.Recent advances in model compression have shown that ternary quantisation (i.e., using only {-1, 0, 1} as weights) substantially reduces memory footprint, inference time, and energy usage of LLMs with minimal performance degradation.However, whether these already efficient models can be further pruned to reduce resource requirements without compromising effectiveness remains unexplored.We investigate this question across six models, four sparsity levels, and six structured and unstructured pruning techniques.We find that even minimal pruning yields substantial efficiency gains: pruning fewer than 5% of parameters reduces inference time and energy consumption by up to 21%, and memory usage by up to 13%, with minimal accuracy degradation.We also find that, for pruned models with less than a 5% accuracy drop, the most energy and inferencetime efficient configurations are achieved by pruning entire attention layers, whereas the most memory efficient configurations are obtained by pruning entire MLP layers.These findings highlight pruning as a complementary technique to ternary quantisation for reducing environmental footprint of LLMs while maintaining model effectiveness.The code is available at: https://github.com/pietrotrope/ TernaryLLMsPruning.

W7224496406.abstract: We introduce OCEANGYM, the first comprehensive benchmark for underwater embodied agents, designed to advance AI in one of the most demanding real-world environments.OCEANGYM features eight realistic task domains and a unified agent framework driven by Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that integrates perception, memory, and sequential decision-making.Agents must follow natural language instructions, interpret optical and sonar inputs, autonomously explore complex environments, and achieve long-horizon goals.Extensive experiments reveal a significant performance gap between state-of-the-art MLLMdriven agents and human experts, underscoring persistent challenges in perception, planning, and adaptation underwater.By offering a high-fidelity, rigorously designed platform, OCEANGYM establishes a testbed for robust embodied AI and represents a foundational step toward sim-to-real transfer on Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs), marking progress toward agents capable of operating in one of Earth's last unexplored frontiers 1 .

W7225010404.abstract: Marine tourism is a strategic sector heavily influenced by tourists' perceptions and experiences, which are captured in user-generated content across various digital platforms. However, the multifaceted, informal, and ambiguous nature of reviews poses challenges for sentiment analysis based on conventional methods. This study proposes an aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) framework using a Large Language Model (LLM) integrated with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) to analyze cross-platform marine tourism reviews. The proposed approach includes text reflection preprocessing, aspect extraction, sentiment classification based on zero-shot and few-shot learning schemes, and XAI integration to improve the interpretability of the results through the contribution of keywords and evidence phrases. Model evaluation is conducted by comparing the model output against reference annotations on a subset of review data using precision, recall, and F1-score metrics at the aspect level. Experimental results show that the zero-shot scheme produces moderate performance with an accuracy and macro-average F1 score of 0.33, while the application of some-shot learning significantly improves performance with an accuracy of 0.87 and a macro-average F1 score of 0.87. The integration of XAI shows that the resulting sentiment prediction model is supported by relevant linguistic evidence, thereby increasing transparency and trust in the analysis results. These findings confirm that the proposed ABSA-based LLM framework is effective, interpretative, and has the potential to be used as a decision-support tool in the management and development of data-driven marine tourism destinations.

W7225067406.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies has accelerated the growth of Islamic financial technology (fintech), enhancing financial accessibility, efficiency, and innovation. However, increasing reliance on automated decision-making systems has raised concerns regarding trust, transparency, accountability, and ethical governance. This study systematically reviews trust formation in AI-driven Islamic financial systems, focusing on the integration of technological and ethical dimensions. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic search identified 1,842 records, of which 34 peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2016 and 2025 met the inclusion criteria. The findings indicate that trust is predominantly influenced by technological factors, including system reliability, perceived security, service quality, and ease of use, alongside governance and regulatory support. In contrast, ethical dimensions such as Shariah compliance, transparency, Maqasid al-Shariah, and niyyah remain underexplored. The review highlights the need for integrated trust frameworks that align technological innovation with Islamic ethical principles to support sustainable and trustworthy fintech ecosystems.

W7225075651.abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has transformed medical oncology, while individual’s therapeutic response to treatment is difficult because of the diverse nature and features of tumors and low precision and accuracy of markers, such as PD-L1, Tumor Mutational Burden (TMB), and Microsatellite Instability (MSI). Artificial intelligence integrates different types of data to cover the complexity of tumor-immune biological mechanisms. This review summarizes the recent studies in AI application in biomarker discovery and cancer immunotherapy prediction from a pan-cancer perspective, summarizing AI techniques, data types, clinical performance metrics, and implementation barriers. Selected AI-derived biomarkers have demonstrated promising performance compared with conventional biomarkers in specific studies. Indeed, selected AI-derived biomarkers demonstrated moderate-to-high discriminatory performance while reported estimates varied according to cancer type, prediction endpoint, and validation design. Deep Learning has shown promising results in Digital Pathology and Radiomics via providing tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes quantification and spatial immune phenotyping. Meanwhile, multi-omics integration frameworks, such as graph neural networks and transformer-based models can reveal complex associations among genomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic data. AI has indicated promising results in predicting both primary and acquired resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors, stratifying potential patients for immunotherapy, and predicting immune-related adverse events. Post-hoc explainability methods, including SHAP and LIME, can provide feature-attribution information, although their outputs should not be interpreted as causal or mechanistic explanations. The intersection of artificial intelligence and cancer immunotherapy is opening new roads for precision-oncology. However, the clinical translation of AI-driven biomarkers requires robust external validation, standardized methodologies, and evaluation across diverse patient populations.

W7225092422.abstract: Abstract Background Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have improved outcomes in advanced clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), but predictive biomarkers are lacking. The role of paired-like homeodomain 1 (PITX1) in ccRCC remains unclear. Methods Machine learning identified PITX1 as a key biomarker. Multi-omics analyses integrated bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq), spatial transcriptomics (ST), data from three randomized controlled trials (IMmotion151, CheckMate025, JAVELIN Renal 101) and West China Hospital ccRCC cohort. Results PITX1 was upregulated in ccRCC, associated with BAP1 mutation and hypomethylation. scRNA-seq and ST revealed the expression patterns of PITX1 in different cell clusters. High PITX1 expression correlated with advanced clinicopathological features, poor survival, and metabolic reprogramming towards glucose and methionine metabolism. Enrichment analysis suggested high PITX1 would lead to more malignant tumor biological behaviors. It shaped an immunosuppressive microenvironment with regulatory T cells (Tregs) infiltrated and elevated immune checkpoints. Crucially, high PITX1 indicates inferior benefits for patients receiving immunotherapy. Conclusion PITX1 is a novel biomarker linked to aggressive tumor behavior, metabolic alteration, and immune evasion, predicting poor response to immunotherapy in ccRCC.

W7225125047.abstract: Large language models act only through the infrastructure that surrounds them. That infrastructure, the harness, determines what a model can accomplish and how it fails, yet it has no settled definition. To address this gap, we decompose the harness into eight functional components that can be specified and compared across systems, and we propose a portable specification framework that records which model ran in which harness. The record is needed because different harness configurations can yield several-fold differences in reported scores for the same model, and because much of an agent's attack surface lies in its harness. Existing model cards and agent cards provide release and operational information, but do not establish the sequence of effective configurations within a run. Harnesses can change between releases and between runs, and, where agents edit their own tools and configuration, within a run. Enacted AI laws contain documentation duties relevant to covered systems, subject to their respective scopes and application dates, but do not prescribe the common harness record proposed here. Therefore, the harness has to be explicitly described and specified as a versioned part of the system.

W7225425849.abstract: Gene therapy and genome editing technologies have revolutionized modern medicine by allowing for the precise correction of genetic defects and novel therapeutic approaches for diseases that were previously considered untreatable. It is a technique that treats or prevents various diseases by replacing, correcting or inactivating faulty genes. Among these technologies, CRISPR-Cas systems have emerged as particularly simple, flexible, and rapidly expanding in their clinical applications. This review aims to synthesize the latest advances in gene therapy and CRISPR technologies, including mechanisms, delivery systems, therapeutic applications, clinical trials, challenges, and future perspectives. Recent developments such as base editing and prime editing have significantly improved the accuracy and safety of genome modification approaches. In addition, advances in viral and non-viral delivery systems have enhanced the efficiency of therapeutic gene transfer into target tissues. Current clinical trials have demonstrated promising outcomes in the treatment of inherited blood disorders, cancers, and metabolic diseases. The integration of artificial intelligence and bioinformatics tools is also improving guided RNA design and minimizing off-target effects in genome editing applications. Ethical considerations and regulatory frameworks remain essential for ensuring the safe and equitable implementation of these technologies in clinical practice. We conclude that despite the hurdles, high costs, long term safety monitoring, and immune system reactions to vectors, CRISPR-based strategies are on the verge of revolutionizing the practice of medicine with innovative, accurate solutions to hard hereditary, oncologic, and infectious diseases.

W7225538965.abstract: Innovation in clinical microbiology is urgently needed in response to the global disease burden caused by microbial organisms and increasing antimicrobial resistance (AMR). Machine learning, deep learning and natural language processing technologies are quickly changing the way clinical pathology labs identify organisms, predict resistance and perform disease surveillance. A narrative review was performed using peer reviewed articles published between 2020-2025. Articles were identified using PubMed, Embase and Web of Science databases using specific MeSH terms and keywords relating to AI, machine learning, deep learning, clinical microbiology, antimicrobial resistance and disease surveillance. AI has been shown to be highly accurate with >95% accuracy with identifying species and predicting resistance phenotypes from mass spectrometry and whole genome sequencing data. Convolutional neural networks for microscopy have shown high sensitivity and specificity when compared to experts. Natural language processing has been used to extract information from electronic health records and global text to predict outbreaks days in advance. Federated learning and explainable AI are being developed to overcome privacy, regulation and trust issues. AI is a game changer in the field of clinical microbiology. It allows faster diagnosis, improved antimicrobial stewardship and improved global responses. Carefully curated global data sets, regulation and equitable implementation will ensure the true potential of AI will be realised, particularly in low and middle income countries.
